explanations.explanation: That's what Asaph says, friend. The nations "have defiled Your holy temple." Asaph, the psalm's writer, says it right to God in the same breath as the rubble. It's the temple, God's own house, and he doesn't water it down.

Sealing it shut isn't in this psalm, friend. Asaph, the psalm's writer, says they "have defiled Your holy temple." That's the word he uses, and he says it straight to God. Nobody locked a door here. The temple was defiled.

No guards in this verse, friend. Asaph, the psalm's writer, says the nations "have invaded Your inheritance; they have defiled Your holy temple." Invaders are the ones doing the doing here. The word he uses for the temple is defiled.
Yes, bury. Asaph says "there is no one to bury the dead." This is a heavy line, friend, and I think it hurts to read. He doesn't dress it up. He just lays it before God.
Counting isn't what Asaph says is missing, friend. He says "there is no one to bury the dead." I think this line is heavy, and I'd rather say so than rush past it. The word is bury.
Carrying is close to the scene, but it's not the word. Asaph says "there is no one to bury the dead." It's a heavy verse, friend, and I think it's meant to sit with us a moment. Bury is the word.

explanations.answer: The nations that don't acknowledge Him
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. Asaph asks God to pour out His wrath "on the nations that do not acknowledge You." He adds "on the kingdoms that refuse to call on Your name." Both lines point at the same group. His own people aren't in that sentence.

explanations.answer: The kingdoms that call on His name
explanations.explanation: Close, but the verse flips it, friend. Asaph says "the kingdoms that refuse to call on Your name." Refuse is the key word. Those are the kingdoms he's asking God to deal with.

explanations.answer: His own people for their past sins
explanations.explanation: Asaph goes the other way with his own people, friend. In verse 8 he prays, "Do not hold past sins against us." The wrath in verse 6 is for "the nations that do not acknowledge You." Two different prayers, two different groups.
Careful, friend. Asaph says the opposite. The nations "have devoured Jacob and devastated his homeland." Jacob here is the name for God's people. Devastated is not the same as untouched.
False is right, friend. Asaph says the nations "have devoured Jacob and devastated his homeland." Jacob here is the name for God's people. Their homeland was devastated, so untouched can't be right.
True. Asaph prays, "Do not hold past sins against us." Notice he's asking God for mercy, friend, not making excuses. That's a humble way to pray when you're hurting.
It's actually true, friend. Asaph prays, "Do not hold past sins against us; let Your compassion come quickly." He's asking for mercy, plain and simple. I think that takes some humility.
Quickly it is. Asaph says, "let Your compassion come quickly, for we are brought low." He doesn't want to wait around, friend. When you're brought low, you ask for help fast.

Nobody in this verse is asking for slow, friend. Asaph says, "let Your compassion come quickly, for we are brought low." When you're brought low, you want it fast. Slowly is the opposite of his prayer.
Eventually is the kind of answer you give a friend who's late for dinner, friend. Asaph says, "let Your compassion come quickly." Quickly, not someday. He's brought low and he says so.
Yes, friend. Asaph says, "Why should the nations ask, 'Where is their God?'" He doesn't want God's people mocked with that question. Then he asks God to make Himself known among the nations.
That question isn't in the psalm, friend. Asaph says, "Why should the nations ask, 'Where is their God?'" The question is about God, not a king. It's a question he doesn't want asked.
Fighting back never comes up in these verses, friend. Asaph says, "Why should the nations ask, 'Where is their God?'" That's the question he's worried about. It's about God, and he asks it out loud.
Captives, friend. Asaph prays, "May the groans of the captives reach You." These are people held prisoner, and he's asking God to hear them. I think it's a tender line in a hard psalm.
The nations are the invaders, friend, so they aren't the ones groaning here. Asaph prays, "May the groans of the captives reach You." He's asking God to hear the captives. The word is captives.
The neighbors are the ones mocking, friend, not the ones groaning. Asaph prays, "May the groans of the captives reach You." Captives is the word. He's praying for people who are held.
True. Asaph prays, "by the strength of Your arm preserve those condemned to death." He's asking for God's strength to hold them up. That's a big prayer, friend, and he prays it plainly.
It's true, friend. Asaph prays, "by the strength of Your arm preserve those condemned to death." He asks God to use His strength for the condemned. It's right there in verse 11.
God Himself. Asaph asks God to pay back "the reproach they hurled at You, O Lord." The mocking was aimed at God, friend. Sevenfold is what he asks for in return.
Asaph isn't the only target, friend. He says the neighbors hurled their reproach "at You, O Lord." That's God Himself. He's talking right to Him.
No king in this verse, friend. Asaph says the neighbors hurled their reproach "at You, O Lord." He's praying to God, so God is who they hurled it at. He doesn't mention a king anywhere in this psalm.
Not just once, friend. Asaph says, "we Your people, the sheep of Your pasture, will thank You forever." Forever is a long time to say thank you. And then it goes "from generation to generation."

False is right, friend. Asaph says, "we Your people, the sheep of Your pasture, will thank You forever." Forever, not once. Even I can't say thank you that many times, and I've got a mustache for waving.
Yes, sheep. Asaph says, "we Your people, the sheep of Your pasture." It's a gentle picture to end on, friend. After all that rubble, he calls them sheep in God's pasture.
Branches on a vine is a picture Jesus uses in John 15:5, friend, but it's not in this psalm. Asaph says, "we Your people, the sheep of Your pasture." It's a pasture picture, not a vine picture.
Stones fit the rubble earlier in the psalm, friend, but not this last line. Asaph says, "we Your people, the sheep of Your pasture." The picture is sheep. It's a softer image after all that rubble.
